title: Read any ISO-8601 value

blocks.text: `java.time` has one class per kind of value, and each prints and parses ISO-8601 by default. A value's ISO text shows which kind it is:

rows: a date and time with no zone: `LocalDateTime`
a point on the UTC timeline: `Instant`
a date-time with a UTC offset: `OffsetDateTime`
a date-time in a region zone: `ZonedDateTime`

blocks.text: Write `IsoText.read(String text)`. It returns the value that `text` spells, as an object of the class in the table (declared return type `Object`).

items: A trailing `Z` means UTC: that is an `Instant`.
An offset such as `+05:30` with no zone ID is an `OffsetDateTime`; the same text followed by a zone ID in brackets is a `ZonedDateTime`.
An amount starts with `P`. One with a time part (a `T`) is a `Duration`; one without is a `Period`.

cases.says: A date, a time, a date-time and a UTC instant each come back as the type that fits them.
A date-time with a +05:30 offset and no zone ID is an OffsetDateTime.
A date-time followed by a zone ID in brackets is a ZonedDateTime in that zone.
PT2H30M is a Duration and P1Y2M3D is a Period.

concepts: Duration is a time-based amount (hours, minutes, seconds) and Period a date-based one (years, months, days).
java.time prints ISO-8601 from toString() and parses it by default, so each type has its own recognisable text form.
Local, offset and zoned date-times and instants are different types, chosen by whether a value carries no zone, an offset, a region zone or is a UTC point.
